elowen.title: Bedside Manner
elowen.text:
Elowen asks you to come by for an afternoon check-up. She says it's routine, although she has never mentioned a routine before.

She has you sit behind the curtain of drying herbs in the corner she's made into a clinic. She listens to your chest and looks at your tongue. All the while she talks, quickly, about willow tincture and the mountain wind and a dock worker's sprained wrist. Sprigs of rosemary keep slipping out of her braid.

Your breathing is ordinary. So is everything else. She takes your pulse last, with two cool fingers on your wrist, and counts.

She finishes counting. Her fingers stay where they are.

"It's very steady," she says to the floorboards. Then, more quietly: "I walked into this town with a letter for a physician who had been dead six years. I've been on my own a long while, Sam. Hollowmere feels much less empty with you across the desk."
ngpp: When her fingers settle over your wrist, she stops. She looks at them, surprised, as if they already knew the rhythm before she counted. She says it must be a coincidence, and she doesn't count it.

"Forgive me, Sam." Her ears go pink as she pours the tea without asking how you take it. She has it right. "My hands seem to know your pulse far better than our acquaintance allows, and I can't think why."

She skips the pretext this time. Her fingers stay on your wrist, steady and unashamed. "I cannot say when I first measured this beat, Sam. Only that every life leads me back to your table. I am sure of it."

choices.label: Tell her the distance feels shorter to you too
choices.res: "It feels shorter to me too," you say. She keeps her fingers on your wrist and doesn't count anything. The tea goes cold between you. Her ears turn pink, then pinker, and she looks up from the floorboards at last. Her green eyes are wet and steady. Neither of you says what the silence is for, and neither of you ends it.

choices.label: Offer to be her patient any time
choices.res: "Any time," you say. {N} hides behind her sleeve, ears pink to the tips. She mumbles that a patient should really attend weekly, for continuity of care. She is already writing "weekly" in her notes before you can see it. When you stand to go she hands you a sprig of rosemary, as if it were a prescription.

image.comp: pressing a stethoscope-like charm to his chest, nervously babbling about herbs
image.setting: small infirmary with herbs drying from the rafters

elowen.title: Tea Service
elowen.text:
Elowen brings tea up to your room in the evening, as she has started doing, with the tray held carefully in both hands and a little steam rising off the pot.

She knocks with her elbow and comes in on the knock. That has never mattered before. Tonight you're halfway through changing your shirt.

She sees.

The tray hits the floor. Porcelain goes everywhere, and the smell of mint and lemon balm comes up off the rug. You stand frozen with one arm in a sleeve. She stands frozen with her hands still shaped around a tray that is no longer there. Her ears are turning red from the tips down.

Neither of you breathes. A cup that somehow survived rolls slowly across the boards and comes to rest against your foot.

1.title: Herb Oil & Steam
1.text:
Elowen knocks properly this time and waits to be asked in. She has a warm clay vial of rosemary oil in one hand and two cups of lemon-balm tea balanced in the other.

You're half-dressed from the washroom. Her ears flush, and she looks, and she doesn't run.

"Your shoulders have been knotted all week, Sam. I can see it in how you carry the ledgers." She sets the cups down on the sill, where they'll be safe, and pulls the cork with her thumb. "If you'd sit on the edge of the bed, I could do something about it. I promise not to drop anything tonight."

choices.label: Let her warm oiled hands work your shoulders—and return the favor
choices.res: You sit on the edge of the bed and let her warm, oiled hands go to work on your shoulders. The knots give one by one. When she's done you take the vial and turn her around. You knead her slender shoulders, slow, until Elowen tips her head back against your collarbone with a breathless sigh. Her braid brushes your arm. She doesn't ask you to stop.
choices.fallbackRes: Her hands slide down your back and stop low, between the shoulder blades. Her breath catches. She rests her forehead against you, ears burning crimson, and stays there a while. The rosemary oil is warm in the air. "This is not strictly part of the treatment," she whispers into your shirt. She doesn't move, and neither do you.

choices.label: Thank her and drink the lemon balm while she rests
choices.res: "Thank you," you say, and take the cup, and sit. She pours two steady cups without spilling a drop, visibly proud of herself. She tucks her knees up on the quilt beside yours. You drink the lemon balm while she rests her head against the wall and tells you which of the dock workers has a bad shoulder. It is the first time she has sat on your bed.

3.title: Chamomile & Bare Skin
3.text:
Elowen doesn't bring a tray tonight. She meets you in the washroom, where the tub is already full and the steam smells of rosemary.

She's wearing a loose linen shift and nothing else. It has gone damp and clings to her tits and her hips, and she knows it does. She doesn't cover herself. Her ears are pink and her green eyes stay on yours.

"Medical advice, Sam. You are far too tense." She draws the shift's lacing loose with one finger. "Tonight the healer prescribes both hands, and she intends to supervise the whole treatment."

choices.label: Pull her bare into the warm oil and water
choices.res: You pull her into the warm water, and the wet linen peels off her shoulders in your hands. Elowen lets it go. The oil is slick and sweet, and her freckled skin is pink with the heat. She wraps her arms around your neck and kisses you, deep and clumsy and happy, while rosemary steam rises around you both. She whispers that she has wanted this for weeks.

choices.label: Hold her close in the tub and kiss her slowly
choices.res: You slip into the tub behind her and draw her back against your chest. She melts into the rosemary water with a sigh. Your lips find her neck and the tip of one long ear, and she shivers and turns her head to be kissed properly. Her hand finds yours under the water and holds it. Nobody speaks for a long time.

choices.label: Laugh it off
choices.res: You laugh. She laughs too, eventually, from behind both hands, shoulders shaking. Then you both kneel and pick up the shards, not quite looking up. She says it's the fourth teapot this season. You say you'll buy a sturdier one. She says the problem was never the teapot, and goes pink all the way to her braid.

choices.label: Apologize profusely
choices.res: You apologize. She apologizes back. You both bow in turn for ten minutes, like two clockwork birds, saying sorry to the floor and then the tray. In the end she covers her mouth and laughs, and you do too. The broken teapot is never mentioned again, but she knocks twice now, and waits to be told to come in.

choices.label: "You're a healer. You've seen it all, right?"
choices.res: "Not... all," she says faintly. She fans her flushed face with one hand and doesn't look away, which is more than she has managed all month. "I have seen a great many patients. None of them were you." She picks up a shard of porcelain, studies it, and sets it down again, her fingers not quite steady.

else.res: She turns red to the tips of her pointed ears. She mutters something about anatomy textbooks and how they are not at all the same, and then she kneels very fast to gather the shattered cups. She keeps her back to you the whole time. Whatever she says to the teapot is too quiet to hear. She doesn't bring tea for two days.

image.comp: dropping a tea tray in a doorway, hands over her face, peeking through her fingers
image.setting: small bedroom, spilled tea on the floor

elowen.title: Flower Crowns
elowen.text:
You go out past the walls with Elowen to gather herbs. She has a basket on her arm and a list in her neat hand: yarrow, feverfew, and something for the cook's cough.

For the first hour you do gather herbs. She shows you which leaves to take and which to leave for next year, and she's patient when you bring her the wrong plant twice.

Somewhere in the second hour the list is forgotten. The meadow smells of crushed clover and the sun is warm. Elowen sits down in the grass and weaves you a flower crown, with the same quick, careful fingers that tie off a bandage. She sets it on your head and adjusts it very seriously.

You make her one back. It's terrible. It's lopsided, and it sheds petals when you lift it.

She wears it all day. She wears it back through the town gate, past the guards, with her chin up.

choices.label: Pull her down into the clover when you're both alone
choices.res: Far from the road, behind tall sunlit grass, Elowen lets the herb basket tip over. She laughs, soft and a little scared, and pulls you down onto her cloak. Yarrow spills across the clover. She takes the crown off her braid and sets it on your chest, and then her hands go to your shirt. "Nobody can see us," she says, as if asking.

choices.label: Wear her crown home
choices.res: You wear her crown home through the gate, with pollen on your collar, and you don't mind the guards' stares. She walks half a step closer than usual. At the first corner she reaches over and straightens a petal that has fallen over your eye, and doesn't take her hand back for a while. Her ears are pink the whole way.

choices.label: Tell her the lopsided one suits her
choices.res: "It suits you," you say, about your own wreck. {N} adjusts it on her braid with immense seriousness, sheds three petals, and declares it the finest crown in Hollowmere. You say you've seen better. She says she hasn't. She keeps it on for the rest of the afternoon, and looks at you sideways every time a petal falls.

image.comp: placing a flower crown on his head in a meadow, holding the lopsided one he made her
image.setting: wildflower meadow outside town walls, sunny afternoon

elowen.title: Burnout
elowen.text:
For weeks Elowen has been going down to the docks every night after her work at the house is done. She treats the dock workers for free. She comes home near dawn with salt on her hem and shadows under her eyes, and she says she isn't tired.

Nobody asked her to do it. She saw that the dock had no healer, and she couldn't leave it alone.

Today she collapses in the kitchen, in the middle of a sentence about willow bark. You catch her before she reaches the floor. She weighs almost nothing. The sprig of rosemary has come loose from her braid, and her hands are cold.

She comes round with her head on your arm and tries to sit up straight away.

"I'm quite all right," she says. "I only need a moment. There's a man with a crushed foot who's expecting me at six."
ngpp: You catch her before she hits the floor, and she blinks up at you with sleepy recognition. For a second it's as if she has dreamed this already, a wool blanket round her knees and your voice nearby.
"Don't scold me yet, Sam," she mumbles against your hoodie, her fingers tight in your sleeve. "I think I know how stubbornly you insist on soup. I think I have lost this argument before."
Even exhausted, Elowen tucks her cold fingers inside your collar, with complete trust. "I knew you wouldn't let me sleep on the floorboards, Sam. Same as always. I remember. Please, just the soup."

choices.label: Scold her
choices.res: You scold her. She cries. Not because you're wrong, which makes it worse. The rosemary stays on the floor where it fell, and she doesn't speak to you until morning. At dawn you find a cup of tea outside your door, still warm, and a note that says "I am sorry. You are right. I still have a man with a foot."

choices.label: Take care of her for a day
choices.res: You make soup, badly. You read to her from the apothecary's herbal, doing the voices, also badly. You don't leave her side. She sleeps for fourteen hours with one hand curled in your sleeve, and when she wakes she looks at the ceiling, and then at you, and doesn't try to get up for the first time in weeks. You sit there.

choices.label: Fund a free clinic night (150g)
choices.res: You pay for it. One night a week, with help from the apothecary's apprentices, and a proper cot and clean linen for the dock workers. She hugs you so hard your ribs creak. She presses her damp face against your hoodie and says thank you into it, several times, getting quieter each time. She doesn't let go for a while.

cantAfford.res: You can't afford it, and you tell her so. She takes your hand and thanks you for trying. "It is more than anyone else has offered, Sam." She says she will keep going to the docks on her own, but only three nights a week, and she makes you promise to check.

image.comp: collapsed against kitchen cabinets, exhausted, healer's satchel spilled, the man kneeling beside her

elowen.title: Starlight
elowen.text:
Elowen leads you up the windy ridge above Hollowmere on a night so clear that both moons throw shadows. She spreads her travelling cloak over the cool clover and sits, and pats the place beside her.

Then she teaches you her sky. She names the constellations of the cedar glade where she was born, one at a time, in quiet silver syllables you can't pronounce. There's the Loom, and the Heron, and the Two Sisters Who Would Not Speak. Each one has a story, and each story is older than the town below you.

She touches your sleeve each time she points, so that you'll look in the right place.

As she talks, her shoulders come down. Her voice gets softer and steadier. You understand that she hasn't said these names aloud to anyone in a very long time, and that she kept them until she had someone to give them to.

2.text:
Elowen leads you up the quiet ridge above Hollowmere and spreads her cloak over the clover. Tonight she doesn't sit beside you. She curls straight in against your shoulder, as if she's been waiting all day to do it.

She still names her homeland's constellations for you, in soft silver syllables: the Loom, the Heron, the Two Sisters. But she keeps losing her place. Every few names she turns her warm face into your collar and stays there.

"I've forgotten which one comes next," she admits against your neck. She doesn't sound sorry about it. Her hand has found its way under your hoodie and is resting flat on your chest, over your heartbeat.

choices.label: Listen to every single one
choices.res: There are dozens of constellations, and you stay quiet for every story. By the final horizon star her cheek rests against your collarbone. She stops pointing at the sky. She just keeps saying the names, softly, to your sleeve, until the Heron is the last one left, and she says it twice, as if she were setting it down.

choices.label: Make up a constellation for her
choices.res: "The Clumsy Healer," you say, and trace it in the sky. She shoves your ribs. She tells you that's not a real shape and that it's offensive to the Two Sisters. The next morning she copies it into the margin of her star chart, in neat silver ink, and doesn't mention it. You only find it when she leaves the book open.

choices.label: Kiss her softly beneath the open sky
choices.res: Elowen draws a sharp breath as you turn her chin toward yours, under both moons. Her eyes are very wide. Then they close, and she kisses you, shy and then not shy at all, her fingers gripping the front of your hoodie. She pulls you down onto the warm wool cloak, and the stars go on reciting themselves above you.

image.comp: pointing up at the night sky from a hilltop, naming constellations, the man beside her
image.setting: grassy hilltop at night, sweeping starry sky

elowen.title: Long-Lived
elowen.text:
Elowen asks you to come and look at the herb garden after dusk. There's nothing to see. It's dark, and moths are circling the lamp over the bench.

She kisses you. It's very quick and it lands slightly off-center. Then she hides her face in the front of your shirt.

"Elves live a long time," she mumbles into the grey cotton. "I'm a hundred and eighteen. For most of that, people have only come to me when something hurt." Her fingers tighten in your sleeve. "You'll be gone long before I am. I've done the sums, and I did them again to be sure. I would still like to spend some of my time with you, Sam. As much as you'll give me."

Her braid smells of rosemary and rain.

She doesn't let go of your hand all the way back to her room, and at the door she doesn't let go of it either.
ngpp: She leads you up the stairs, and her grip doesn't hesitate. She knows each bend of the hall without looking, as though another heart inside hers has walked it already, and she lets it lead her.

"Elves measure years differently," she whispers against your shirt, smiling, unsteady. "So why does it feel as though I have waited several lifetimes for this evening, Sam? I cannot make the sums come out."
"No erased cycle can take away what my chest remembers," Elowen whispers against your neck as she closes the door. "I have lived a long time, Sam. Every year I have left belongs here, with you."
elowen.goLead: In her bedroom, among the hanging herbs, Elowen shuts the door quietly and lifts her face into your hands. She's trembling a little, and her braid has slipped forward over one bare shoulder.

choices.label: Say yes
Not yet
choices.res: {N} nods against your chest, embarrassed and relieved. "I can wait. Don't make it too long." She is still holding your sleeve. She lets go one finger at a time and walks you to the stair, hand over her mouth. "I'm not sorry I asked," she says. "Only that I'm slow."
